Get started

Build a game with Odin and Godot

3 min readOdin × GodotPage source ↓
On this page ↓
Choose a starting pointHow a script runsLearn the scripting surfaceChoose a multiplayer modelStudy a complete game

odin_godot adds compiled Odin scripts to Godot. You author scenes in the Godot editor, attach .odin files to nodes, and use typed bindings to call the engine. The same SDK includes two independent multiplayer frameworks: Kit and Replay.

Start with a running scene. Choose a networking model once the game has state and an interaction worth synchronizing.

Choose a starting point#

What you want to build Start here What you will have
Your first Odin script Install the SDK, then write a script A compiled script attached to a Godot node, with an Inspector property and a frame callback
Odin gameplay in an existing Godot project Add the SDK to your project The addon, scripts library, and editor settings connected to your project
A cooperative game with object-based state Build a Kit game Two players, owner-streamed movement, and authority-owned shared state
A game whose complete simulation can be restored Build a Replay game A typed world with recorded input, correction, and detached Godot views
A desktop or browser release Build and export A plan for compiling, packaging, and checking the target build

How a script runs#

An Odin script has three pieces: a struct holding script state, free procedures implementing behavior, and an engine node stored in the struct's owner field. The build generates registration and compiles your scripts into a library. The core GDExtension registers the Odin script language with Godot and loads that library.

Godot still owns the scene tree, rendering, input devices, animation, and audio. You decide which gameplay values live in scripts and, when using Replay, which values belong in the restorable world.

Learn the scripting surface#

The script model maps Godot concepts to Odin structs and procedures. The authoring reference covers lifecycle callbacks, Inspector properties, signals, methods, resources, and cross-script calls. Use the editor workflow for building, reload-on-save, completion, and debugging.

A single-player game can use these facilities directly. A session or timeline is needed only when you choose a framework that owns that part of the game.

Choose a multiplayer model#

Kit declares how fields on registered entities are synchronized. Its commands handle shared interactions. Its simulation lane advances fast state at fixed ticks, predicts local input, and applies authority corrections.

Replay keeps gameplay in a typed World and steps it from recorded inputs. Each retained frame captures the World at one tick. The runner owns this history and applies corrections; Godot nodes display the result without owning simulation state. Replay also has cooperative owner streams and a deterministic peer-input runner. It remains experimental; use its documented support envelope when choosing a shipping configuration.

Read choosing a multiplayer model for the tradeoffs. The visual field guide follows a contested pickup through both designs and lets you inspect a correction one tick at a time.

Study a complete game#

Play Scrapyard in your browser, then use the Replay Scrapyard contributor guide to follow a feature through authored content, simulation, input, and presentation. The examples directory gives smaller starting points for each model.
